foods.name: Adobo
foods.about: Chicken or pork braised in vinegar, soy sauce, garlic and bay leaf. Every family has its own version. Best with plain rice.

foods.name: Sinigang
foods.about: A sour tamarind soup with pork, shrimp or fish and lots of vegetables. Comfort food on a rainy day.

foods.name: Lechon
foods.about: Whole roast pig with crackling skin. Cebu's version is stuffed with lemongrass and needs no sauce.

foods.name: Kinilaw
foods.about: Raw fish cured in vinegar and calamansi with ginger, onion and chili. Ask for it freshly made at coastal markets.

foods.name: Sisig
foods.about: Chopped pork on a sizzling plate with onion, chili and calamansi. A classic with beer.

foods.name: Halo-halo
foods.about: Shaved ice with sweet beans, jelly, fruit, leche flan and ube ice cream. Mix it all up before you eat.

foods.name: Balut
foods.about: A boiled duck egg with a partly developed embryo, sold by street vendors at night. A famous food challenge.

foods.name: Chicken inasal
foods.about: Chicken marinated in calamansi, lemongrass and annatto oil, grilled over charcoal. Eaten with garlic rice.

foods.name: Bicol Express
foods.about: Pork in coconut milk with long green chilis and shrimp paste. The spiciest dish on this list.

foods.name: Vigan empanada
foods.about: A crisp orange shell filled with grated papaya, egg and longganisa. Eat it hot from the stall at Plaza Burgos.

foods.name: Pancit habhab
foods.about: Stir-fried noodles served on a banana leaf, eaten without utensils. Lift the noodles straight to your mouth.

foods.name: Kare-kare
foods.about: Oxtail and vegetables in a thick peanut sauce, served with bagoong (shrimp paste) on the side.

foods.name: Silog (tapsilog)
foods.about: Garlic fried rice and a fried egg with beef tapa, sausage or fish. The standard Filipino breakfast.

foods.name: Taho
foods.about: Warm silken tofu with brown sugar syrup and tapioca pearls, sold in the morning by vendors who call 'Tahooo!'

foods.name: Turon
foods.about: Sweet banana and jackfruit rolled in a spring roll wrapper, fried with caramelised sugar.

foods.name: Durian
foods.about: A strong-smelling fruit with a creamy flesh. Davao is the best place to try it, and it is the star of Kadayawan.

foods.name: Inihaw na liempo
foods.about: Pork belly marinated and grilled over charcoal. The classic inihaw, eaten with rice and a sour dip.

foods.name: Inihaw na bangus
foods.about: Milkfish stuffed with tomato and onion, then grilled. Pangasinan is famous for it.

foods.name: Isaw
foods.about: Grilled chicken or pork intestine on a stick, dipped in spicy vinegar. Cheap and everywhere.

foods.name: Fishball and kikiam
foods.about: Deep-fried fish balls with sweet, sour or spicy sauce, from a street cart.

foods.name: Kwek-kwek
foods.about: Orange-battered, deep-fried quail eggs with vinegar.

foods.name: Lumpiang shanghai
foods.about: Small crisp spring rolls of minced pork. A party favorite.

foods.name: Tinola
foods.about: Light chicken soup with ginger, green papaya and chili leaves.

foods.name: Bulalo
foods.about: Slow-cooked beef shank and bone marrow soup. A cold-weather favorite in Tagaytay.

foods.name: La Paz batchoy
foods.about: Noodle soup with pork innards, crushed chicharon and egg. Born in La Paz market, Iloilo.

foods.name: Pancit Malabon
foods.about: Thick rice noodles in a rich orange seafood sauce with shrimp and egg.

foods.name: Pinakbet
foods.about: Ilocano vegetable stew with squash, okra and eggplant, flavored with bagoong.

foods.name: Laing
foods.about: Dried taro leaves slow-cooked in spicy coconut milk.

foods.name: Pastil
foods.about: Rice with shredded chicken or beef wrapped in a banana leaf. Cheap and filling.

foods.name: Satti
foods.about: Grilled skewers with a sweet, spicy sauce, served with puso rice. A Zamboanga breakfast.

foods.name: Piaya
foods.about: Flat, crisp flatbread filled with muscovado sugar. A Bacolod souvenir.

foods.name: Sans Rival
foods.about: Layered cashew meringue and buttercream cake, sold in Dumaguete.

foods.name: Bibingka
foods.about: Rice cake cooked in banana leaf with coals above and below. Common at Christmas time.

foods.name: Puto bumbong
foods.about: Purple sticky rice steamed in bamboo, with butter, coconut and sugar. A Christmas dawn treat.

foods.name: Ube halaya
foods.about: Sweet purple yam jam. Found in cakes, ice cream and Baguio and Bohol souvenir stores.

festivals.name: Ati-Atihan
festivals.about: Street dancing with soot-painted faces and tribal costumes, honoring the Santo Nino. Expect a very big crowd.

festivals.name: Sinulog
festivals.about: A grand parade and dance honoring the Santo Nino. Book rooms months ahead.

festivals.name: Panagbenga (Flower Festival)
festivals.about: Floral floats and street dancing in the cool mountain city.

festivals.name: Kaamulan
festivals.about: A gathering of seven indigenous groups with rituals, dances and crafts.
festivals.food: Local root crops and grilled meats

festivals.name: Holy Week and Moriones
festivals.about: Masked Roman soldier reenactments. Many cities go quiet, and some shops close on Good Friday.

festivals.name: Pahiyas
festivals.about: Houses decorated with colorful rice wafers (kiping) and fresh produce.

festivals.name: Flores de Mayo
festivals.about: A month of flower offerings and evening processions with the Santacruzan parade.

festivals.name: Parada ng Lechon
festivals.about: Roast pigs dressed in costumes are paraded through the street, and people soak each other with water.

festivals.name: Sandugo
festivals.about: Honors the 1565 blood compact with a week of parades, shows and street dancing.

festivals.name: Kadayawan
festivals.about: A thanksgiving for harvest with tribal costumes, floral parades and street dancing.

festivals.name: Penafrancia Festival
festivals.about: A fluvial procession on the Naga River honoring Our Lady of Penafrancia.

festivals.name: MassKara
festivals.about: Smiling masks, street dancing, and a food fair.

festivals.name: Undas (All Saints' Day)
festivals.about: Families visit cemeteries, bring food and flowers, and stay overnight. Expect heavy travel traffic and full buses and flights.

festivals.name: Giant Lantern Festival
festivals.about: Huge, spinning light-up lanterns made by local artisans.

festivals.name: Simbang Gabi
festivals.about: Nine dawn masses before Christmas, with food stalls outside every church.

festivals.name: Dinagyang
festivals.about: Tribal-dance competition honoring the Santo Nino, with drums, painted bodies and huge costumes. Often called the sister of Ati-Atihan and Sinulog.
festivals.food: La Paz batchoy and fresh seafood

festivals.name: Feast of the Black Nazarene
festivals.about: A huge religious procession of millions of devotees. Very crowded; keep valuables close.

festivals.name: Chinese New Year
festivals.about: The oldest Chinatown in the world comes alive with dragon and lion dances and red lanterns.

festivals.name: Philippine International Hot Air Balloon Festival
festivals.about: Dozens of balloons lift off at sunrise, with a fair and stunt shows.

festivals.name: Pamulinawen Festival
festivals.about: A cultural festival with street dancing named after a famous Ilocano love song.

festivals.name: Araw ng Dabaw
festivals.about: City anniversary with parades, trade fairs and indigenous performances.

festivals.name: Aliwan Fiesta
festivals.about: Competing street dancers and floats from festivals across the country in one weekend.

festivals.name: Bangus Festival
festivals.about: Celebrates milkfish with a grilling contest and street party.

festivals.name: Carabao Festival
festivals.about: Farmers kneel their decorated water buffalo in front of the church to honor San Isidro.

festivals.name: Wattah Wattah Festival
festivals.about: Everyone gets soaked with water in honor of San Juan Bautista, so keep your phone in a dry bag.

festivals.name: Start of the Ber Months
festivals.about: The Philippines begins its Christmas season in September, with songs, lanterns and decorations everywhere.
festivals.food: Bibingka and puto bumbong near the end of the year

festivals.name: Lanzones Festival
festivals.about: Street dancing with fruit-covered floats and free lanzones. Camiguin is famous for its sweet lanzones.

festivals.name: Zamboanga Hermosa Festival
festivals.about: Honors Nuestra Senora del Pilar with a fluvial parade of colorful vinta boats.

festivals.name: Higantes Festival
festivals.about: Giant papier-mache figures dance through the streets for San Clemente.

festivals.name: Noche Buena
festivals.about: The big family Christmas Eve feast after midnight mass.
festivals.food: Hamon, queso de bola and lechon

transport.tip: Say 'Para po' to stop. Pass your fare forward to the driver. Tell the person next to you the stop you want if you are unsure.
Agree on the price before you ride, or ask for the posted rate. A 'special trip' (private) costs more than a shared ride.
Taxis must use the meter. Grab shows a fixed fare up front. Available in Manila, Cebu, Davao, Clark and Angeles.
Choose aircon buses for long trips. Book popular routes ahead during holidays like Holy Week and Undas.
Check the weather and schedules the day before. Trips get cancelled in storms.
Booking weeks ahead gives lower fares. Pack within the baggage limit, because budget carriers charge for extras.
Manila only. Fast in rush hour, but very crowded. Use the stored-value beep card for cheaper rides.

routes.tip: Use the airport queue or book Grab. Skip anyone who approaches you inside the terminal.
Victory Liner and Genesis run frequently. Book ahead during holidays.
Ohayami departs in the evening from Sampaloc. Bring a jacket, because the aircon is cold.
Choose a deluxe bus for sleeper seats.
Pick up from the airport or terminal. The road is long, so take motion sickness pills if you need them.
Take the aircon bus from the South Bus Terminal. They leave every 20-30 minutes.
OceanJet and Weesam Express run many trips. Book on the day or online.
Several trips a day. Get there 30 minutes early for tickets.
Pay the terminal fee and environmental fee at the jetty counters. Official counters have posted rates.
A private van or tricycle costs a lot more. Join a shared van, and ask your hotel about transfers.

scams.title: Taxi with a 'broken' meter
scams.fix: Ask for the meter before you ride ('Pakibukas ang metro po'). If the driver refuses, get out and book Grab or another taxi.

scams.title: Flat-rate airport offers
scams.fix: Drivers approaching you inside arrivals often charge double. Use the official taxi queue or an app.

scams.title: 'Special trip' tricycles and boats
scams.fix: Ask the shared fare first. Say 'Hindi special trip po'. Ask your guesthouse for the usual price.

scams.title: 'The attraction is closed' story
scams.fix: A friendly stranger says your destination is closed and offers a different tour. Check the official page or ask at the entrance yourself.

scams.title: Unofficial tour operators
scams.fix: Book island-hopping, diving and activities through your hotel or a DOT-accredited office. Compare two prices before paying.

scams.title: Short change
scams.fix: Count your change with the cashier, especially with 500 and 1,000 peso bills. Keep small bills for tricycles and jeepneys.

scams.title: Drinks from strangers
scams.fix: Accept drinks only from people you know, and keep your glass in sight, especially at bars and at night.

scams.title: Card skimming and unknown ATMs
scams.fix: Use ATMs inside banks or malls. Cover your PIN. Notify your bank before you travel.

tips.title: Seasons and weather
items: Dry season is roughly Nov-May. It is the best time for beaches.
Rainy season is Jun-Oct, and typhoons are most likely Jul-Oct.
Siargao and Camiguin are best in Mar-Oct, which is the opposite of Palawan.
Check PAGASA forecasts before ferry or island trips.

tips.title: What to pack
items: Light clothes, sunscreen, and a rain jacket
Reef-safe sunscreen and a dry bag for island hopping
A power bank and a universal plug adapter (type A, B and C)
Cash in small bills. Many islands have few ATMs.

tips.title: Etiquette
items: Say 'po' and 'opo' to show respect to elders and strangers.
Do 'mano' (touch an elder's hand to your forehead) if you are invited into a family.
Dress modestly in churches.
Remove shoes when entering a home.
Point with your lips or a nod instead of a finger, which can seem rude.

tips.title: Money
items: Carry cash. Cards work in cities and resorts, but not in small towns.
ATMs charge a fee for foreign cards (often 200-250 pesos). Withdraw larger amounts less often.
Tipping is welcome. About 10% is common at restaurants without a service charge.
Haggle politely at markets, not at fixed-price shops.

tips.title: Connectivity
items: Buy a Globe or Smart SIM at the airport, or use an eSIM.
Mobile data is cheap. Wi-Fi in islands is slow.
Download offline maps before island hops.

tips.title: Entry and documents
items: Many nationalities get 30 days visa-free. Check the rules for your passport.
Register for eTravel before arrival, if it applies to you.
Your passport should be valid for at least 6 months.
Keep a photocopy and a photo of your passport.

fruits.name: Carabao mango
fruits.about: Very sweet yellow mango with a thin seed. Often listed among the world's sweetest.
fruits.why: Eat it ripe, or try the green mango with bagoong.

fruits.name: Calamansi
fruits.about: A tiny sour citrus used in drinks, dips and marinades.
fruits.why: A Philippine kitchen staple, and not often sold fresh abroad. Try it as a juice or in muffins.

fruits.name: Durian
fruits.about: Creamy, strong-smelling flesh. Davao varieties include Puyat and Arancillo.
fruits.why: Davao is the main durian region. Many hotels ban it.

fruits.name: Marang
fruits.about: Soft, sweet white flesh with a honey-like aroma, related to jackfruit.
fruits.why: Rare outside Mindanao and Borneo.

fruits.name: Lanzones
fruits.about: Small round fruit with translucent, sweet and slightly sour segments.
fruits.why: Camiguin has a festival for it every October.

fruits.name: Rambutan
fruits.about: Hairy red shell with juicy white flesh inside.
fruits.why: Common across Southeast Asia, but fresh Mindanao rambutan is good value.

fruits.name: Mangosteen
fruits.about: Purple shell, soft white segments that are sweet and a little tangy.
fruits.why: Often grown in Mindanao. Choose ones with a soft shell.

fruits.name: Pomelo
fruits.about: Huge citrus with mild, juicy segments. Davao pomelo is a local favorite.
fruits.why: Davao pomelo is sweeter than many other kinds.

fruits.name: Pili nut
fruits.about: A creamy nut sold roasted, in candy and in brittle.
fruits.why: Almost entirely a Bicol product. Great as a souvenir.

fruits.name: Langka (jackfruit)
fruits.about: Sweet, chewy yellow pods, eaten fresh or in desserts like halo-halo.
fruits.why: Also used as a vegetable when young (ginataang langka).

fruits.name: Saba banana
fruits.about: Short, starchy banana, never eaten raw like a lakatan. Boiled, fried (banana-cue) or in turon.
fruits.why: Cooking banana for street food, not sold the same way abroad.

fruits.name: Lakatan banana
fruits.about: The standard sweet eating banana in the Philippines.
fruits.why: Cheap and sold by the bunch at every market.

fruits.name: Santol
fruits.about: Round yellow fruit with white pulp that is sour and sweet. Also used in sinigang.
fruits.why: Fresh, pickled or used in cooking.

fruits.name: Atis (sugar apple)
fruits.about: Bumpy green fruit with sweet, custard-like pulp and big black seeds.
fruits.why: Spoon it out and watch for the seeds.

fruits.name: Duhat (Java plum)
fruits.about: Purple berry that stains your tongue. Sweet and puckery.
fruits.why: A seasonal roadside snack, often eaten with salt.

fruits.name: Macopa
fruits.about: Bell-shaped, pale pink fruit that is crisp and watery.
fruits.why: Refreshing on a hot day. Skip it if you want something sweet.

fruits.name: Pineapple
fruits.about: Sweet and juicy, with Bukidnon producing much of the fruit.
fruits.why: The Philippines is among the world's largest producers.

fruits.name: Buko (young coconut)
fruits.about: Fresh coconut water and soft meat, sold roadside with a straw.
fruits.why: Cheap and refreshing everywhere. Buko juice is common.

fruits.name: Chico (sapodilla)
fruits.about: Brown, soft and malty-sweet flesh, like caramel.
fruits.why: Wait until it is soft before you eat it.

fruits.name: Kamias
fruits.about: Small, very sour green fruit used in sinigang and eaten with salt.
fruits.why: Usually cooked, not eaten raw by visitors.

fruits.name: Guyabano (soursop)
fruits.about: Spiky green fruit with creamy, tangy pulp. Often made into juice or ice cream.
fruits.why: Common in juices and smoothies.

cool.title: Cool and dry
cool.sum: The most comfortable time to visit most of the country. The northeast monsoon (amihan) brings cooler, drier air.
regions: Northern Luzon and Cordillera
Dry and cool. Sagada and Banaue can be cold at night, so bring a jacket. Batanes sea can be rough and boats may not sail.
Manila, Bicol and Southern Luzon
Mostly dry. Some rain on the eastern side (Bicol) from the amihan.
Visayas
Good for Cebu, Bohol and Boracay. Eastern parts, such as Samar and Leyte, can still be rainy.
Mindanao
The east (Siargao, Surigao, Davao) can be rainy through February. Davao and Camiguin are usually fine.
Palawan
Dry with calm seas. Very good for island hopping in El Nido and Coron.
tips: Book early for Boracay and El Nido, since this is peak season.
Pack a light jacket for the mountains and for night boat rides.

hot.title: Hot and dry
hot.sum: Hot, sunny and humid. Beaches are at their best, but it can be very hot in the city and crowded during Holy Week.
regions: Northern Luzon and Cordillera
Dry and hot in the lowlands, pleasant in the mountains. Good time for Batanes, Vigan and the rice terraces.
Manila, Bicol and Southern Luzon
Very hot, with heat index often above 40°C. Plan outdoor sights for early morning or late afternoon.
Visayas
Calm seas and clear water. Great for Boracay, Bohol and Moalboal.
Mindanao
Hot and mostly dry. Rains start returning in some areas by late May.
Palawan
Hot with calm seas. Rain usually starts again from May or June.
tips: Holy Week (usually April) is very crowded and many places close for Good Friday.
Drink plenty of water, wear sunscreen, and rest in the afternoon.

early.title: Rainy season starts
early.sum: The southwest monsoon (habagat) brings heavy rain, especially on the western side. Early typhoons are possible, and flooding is common in Metro Manila.
regions: Northern Luzon and Cordillera
Frequent rain and possible landslides on mountain roads. Check road conditions before going to Sagada or Banaue.
Manila, Bicol and Southern Luzon
Heavy rain and flooding in Metro Manila. Bicol can be affected by typhoons.
Visayas
Rain showers, but often drier than Luzon. Boracay's main beach side can have rough seas and flag warnings.
Mindanao
Often less affected by typhoons. Davao and Camiguin may still be good.
Palawan
Rain and rougher sea. Some island hopping tours can be cancelled.
tips: Prices are lower, and fewer people visit.
Keep your flights flexible and keep phones and passports in a dry bag.

peak.title: Typhoon season peak
peak.sum: The busiest months for typhoons. Flights, boats and tours can be cancelled with little notice. Travel is possible, but plan with care.
regions: Northern Luzon and Cordillera
The highest risk. Batanes flights often cancel, and landslides can close the roads to Sagada and Banaue.
Manila, Bicol and Southern Luzon
High risk. Bicol often faces typhoons first, and Manila floods heavily.
Visayas
Moderate to high risk, especially Eastern Visayas. Siargao surf season starts around September.
Mindanao
Usually the safest large region for typhoons, especially the south, but rain and floods still happen.
Palawan
Rainy and rougher seas. Typhoons can pass nearby, and boats can be cancelled.
tips: Buy travel insurance that covers typhoon cancellations.
Avoid tight connections, and add a buffer day before your flight home.
Do not go on boats, hikes or island hopping when a storm signal is up.

late.title: Late rains and typhoons
late.sum: Rain slowly eases, but strong typhoons can still hit, especially Bicol, Visayas and Mindanao's east coast. Christmas season begins.
regions: Northern Luzon and Cordillera
Cooler and drier by December. Good time for Vigan, Sagada and Banaue.
Manila, Bicol and Southern Luzon
Bicol can still be affected by late typhoons in November. Manila is cooler by December.
Visayas
Late typhoons are possible, and have hit the Visayas in November and December in past years. Check forecasts before island hopping.
Mindanao
The east coast can have heavy rain from the northeast monsoon. Siargao surf season continues into November.
Palawan
Improving weather through December, with calmer seas coming back.
tips: December is busy and expensive around Christmas and New Year. Book early.
Check PAGASA before travelling to the Visayas in November.

signals: Strong winds. Minimal to minor threat. Be careful with boats and outdoor tours.
Gale-force winds. Minor to moderate threat. Boat trips are usually stopped.
Storm-force winds. Moderate to significant threat. Stay indoors.
Typhoon-force winds. Significant to severe threat. Stay in a safe building.

faq.a: Many nationalities can enter without a visa for a short stay, often 30 days, but the rules depend on your passport. Check the Bureau of Immigration or the Philippine embassy for your country before you book. Your passport usually needs to be valid for at least six months, and you may be asked to show a ticket out of the country.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit?
faq.a: The drier months, roughly November to May, are usually best for beaches and island hopping. June to October is rainier and has a higher typhoon risk, but it is often cheaper and quieter. Each place has its own best months on the Destinations page, and the typhoon guide on the Safety and phrases page shows the pattern for every month.

faq.q: How does the budget planner work?
faq.a: Tick the places you want to visit, set the days, and choose the activities. Every price is in pesos, per person, and you can edit any of them. The total is shown in pesos and in your own currency. Your choices are saved in your browser, so they are still there when you come back.
No. They are rough estimates to help you plan. Prices change with the season, the place and how you travel, so check current prices before you book. International flights are not included.

The Philippine peso. ATMs are easy to find in cities and malls, but small towns and islands can have none, so bring enough cash for those days. Small bills and coins help for tricycles, jeepneys and market stalls. Cards are accepted in most hotels, malls and larger restaurants.

faq.q: Is it safe to travel in the Philippines?
faq.a: Most visitors travel without problems. Use the same care you would anywhere: watch your bag in crowds, use licensed taxis or ride-hailing apps, and avoid showing valuables. Some areas have government travel advisories, so check your own government's advice for the regions you plan to visit. The Safety and phrases page lists the emergency numbers.

faq.q: How do I get between islands?
faq.a: By plane, ferry or bus-and-ferry combinations. Flights are fastest between far-apart places, and ferries link many nearby islands. Weather can delay both, especially in typhoon season, so keep a spare day before your flight home. See the Getting around page for fares and common routes.

faq.q: Do I need a SIM card or internet?
faq.a: A local SIM or an eSIM is cheap and works well in cities and towns. Coverage can be weak on remote islands and in the mountains, so download offline maps and keep your key bookings saved on your phone.

faq.q: What plug and voltage do they use?
faq.a: The Philippines uses 220 V at 60 Hz. Sockets take flat two-pin plugs (types A and B), and type C is also common. Check that your devices accept 220 V, and bring a universal adapter if you are unsure.

faq.q: Where do the photos and live information come from?
faq.a: Photos come from Wikipedia and Wikimedia Commons, weather from Open-Meteo and exchange rates from Frankfurter. They need an internet connection. If one is not available, the site shows a fallback such as an approximate rate or an emoji instead of a photo.

If photos, the map or the live rate are missing, check your internet connection. If the whole page says it could not load data.json, open the site through a local server such as VS Code Live Server instead of double-clicking the HTML file.
